nameStory: American dragonhead gets its dramatic name from the shape of its individual flowers, which look like tiny dragon heads with open mouths when viewed from the side. The scientific name Dracocephalum literally means 'dragon head' in Latin, making this one of those delightful cases where the common name and scientific name tell the same story!
description: American dragonhead is a small, branching member of the mint family that grows as either a short-lived annual or biennial plant. It produces clusters of tiny pink to violet flowers arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem tips, creating compact flower heads. The plant has the characteristic square stems of the mint family and typically grows low to the ground with multiple branching stems radiating outward.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to violet flowers clustered in tight whorls at stem tips, each individual flower resembling a tiny dragon's head with an open mouth when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant with multiple branching stems spreading outward, typically forming small mats or clumps rather than growing tall and upright

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when rolled between your fingers, a telltale sign of the mint family

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny dark seeds about the size of a pinhead that feel slightly oily to the touch and have a rich, nutty aroma when crushed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, opposite leaves (paired across from each other on the stem) that may have a faint minty or herbal scent when gently crushed

habitat: In New England, American dragonhead is extremely rare, typically found in disturbed soils, sandy areas, or open fields with well-drained conditions. Given its rarity in our region (with only one recorded observation), it's more likely to be encountered as a waif or temporary introduction rather than an established population.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin developing their characteristic branching structure and opposite leaves on square stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the distinctive pink to violet dragon-head flowers appear in whorls at the stem tips, making identification easiest.
seasonality.fall: Plants set seed and begin to decline, with the tiny dark, oily seeds becoming mature and ready for dispersal.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil; biennial plants may persist as small rosettes under snow cover.

funFact: The seeds of American dragonhead are so rich in oil (about 20% oil content) that researchers have seriously studied this little wildflower as a potential commercial birdseed crop for Alaska, where it thrives in harsh conditions that would kill other oil-rich plants!
confusionNotes: American dragonhead might be confused with other small mints, but the distinctive dragon-head shaped flowers clustered in tight whorls at stem tips set it apart. Remember: if the flowers don't look like tiny dragon heads breathing fire, it's probably a different mint!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'American dragonhead,' this plant is incredibly rare in New England and much more common in western North America and the Great Lakes region. Finding one here would be a truly exceptional discovery worth documenting and reporting to local botanists.
compareHints: American dragonhead is the only Dracocephalum species documented in New England. Compared to other small mints in our region, it's distinguished by its unique dragon-head shaped flowers and extremely low, mat-forming growth habit. Most other regional mints either grow more upright or have differently shaped flowers that lack the distinctive dragon-head appearance.
